concepts.def: The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Structures & Functions in Living Organisms — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Structures & Functions in Living Organisms brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Structures & Functions in Living Organisms.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
options: Human skin cell
Yeast
Bacterium
Onion cell
protein synthesis
photosynthesis
aerobic respiration
cell division

mcqs.q: What distinguishes the innate from the adaptive immune response?
options: Innate immunity only works in children; adaptive only works in adults.
Innate immunity attacks viruses and adaptive attacks bacteria.
Innate is fast, non-specific, and has no memory; adaptive is slower initially, highly specific, and forms memory cells.
Antibodies bind to any antigen they meet first.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Innate immunity only works in children; adaptive only works in adults.
Active transport requires energy (ATP) and can move substances against the concentration gradient.
Both move substances down a concentration gradient, but active transport is faster.

mcqs.q: What makes the antigen-binding site of an antibody specific to one antigen?
options: Antibodies bind to any antigen they meet first.
The variable region — its amino acid sequence (and thus shape) differs between antibodies, complementing a specific antigen.
Innate immunity only works in children; adaptive only works in adults.
All antibodies have the same binding site; specificity comes from where they go in the body.
